scriptTitle: Compound Interest, Drawn So You Can Actually See It
script:
[Stick figure holding one coin]
This is Sam. Sam has two hundred dollars a month to put away, and a question: does starting early really matter that much?

[Draw a second, identical stick figure]
This is also Sam, in another timeline. Same job. Same two hundred dollars. One difference: this Sam waits ten years to start.

[Timeline: 40 years vs 30 years. Small print, kept on screen through both totals: $200 paid in at the end of each month; 7% a year, compounded monthly (7% ÷ 12 each month).]
Let's give both of them the same made-up return, seven percent a year, every year. Real life is bumpier. This is only to show the maths.

[Early Sam's pile grows slowly, then fast]
Early Sam saves for forty years. Total paid in: ninety-six thousand dollars. Total at the end: about five hundred and twenty-five thousand.

[Late Sam's pile]
Late Sam saves for thirty years. Total paid in: seventy-two thousand. Total at the end: about two hundred and forty-four thousand.

[Put the piles side by side]
Look at that. Early Sam paid in only twenty-four thousand dollars more, and finished with more than double.

[Zoom into the curve]
Here's why. Interest is paid on your money. Then next year, interest is paid on your money and on last year's interest. The pile earns, and then the earnings earn.

[Rule of 72 on a chalkboard]
A shortcut: divide seventy-two by the yearly rate. At seven percent, that's about ten years to double. So ten extra years isn't ten years of saving. It's one whole extra doubling.

[Both Sams wave]
That's compound interest. It isn't a trick, and it isn't a promise about any investment. It's just what happens when growth is left alone for a long time.

Next time: where money actually comes from. Mostly, it isn't the printer.

With 7% as a true yearly rate and monthly deposits, the totals are $494,308 and $233,891. With one $2,400 deposit at the end of each year they are $479,124 and $226,706. With the deposit at the start of each year they are $512,663 and $242,575. If the monthly deposit lands at the start of the month instead of the end, the totals are $528,025 and $245,417, so the end-of-month detail matters too. The first checker's wording '7% a year, added monthly' is ambiguous: it could be read as 7% added every month, or as the $200 being what is added. 'Compounded monthly (7% ÷ 12 each month)' is the standard phrase and matches the figures exactly. With this note on screen, no spoken number needs to change. The line 'then next year, interest is paid on...' still describes compounding once a year, but that is acceptable as a simplified explanation once the note is visible.

scriptTitle: Kodak Invented the Digital Camera. It Still Went Bankrupt.
script:
[Black screen. One line of text: "Rochester, New York. 1975."]
In 1975, a young engineer at Kodak named Steven Sasson built a strange machine out of spare parts. It was the size of a toaster. It took twenty-three seconds to record one black-and-white picture onto a cassette tape.

[Drawing of the prototype, made for this film (or Kodak's own photo, licensed and credited)]
The picture was tiny, about a hundredth of a megapixel. But there was no film in it. It was the first self-contained digital camera.

[Boardroom illustration]
Sasson showed it to Kodak's managers and executives. Their reaction, as he later told it, was polite, and worried. Kodak made its money from film, paper and chemicals. Most photographs taken in America were, in some way, a small payment to Kodak. A camera with no film was a camera with no payment.

[Text: "That's cute — but don't tell anyone about it." (Steven Sasson, recalling management's reaction)]
So the camera stayed in the lab. Kodak patented it, but never sold it.

[Graph: film sales rising through the 1980s and 1990s]
For a long time, that looked like the right call. Film kept selling. Kodak stayed one of the most recognised names in the world.

[Graph bends]
Then digital cameras got good enough. Kodak sold them too, and by 2005 it sold more of them in America than anyone else. Then they got cheap. Then they moved into phones, and camera sales began to fall.

[Text: "January 2012."]
In January 2012, Kodak filed for bankruptcy protection.

[Slow push in on the prototype]
Kodak didn't miss the future. It built the future, in its own lab, thirty-six years before it went bankrupt. What it couldn't do was make the new thing pay the way the old thing did.

[Title card]
This is Rise and Ruin Files. In the rest of this film: the patents Kodak held, the money it made from them, and the moment it was already too late.

history.reason: Thirty-seven years is the gap to the bankruptcy, not how early the camera was: digital outsold film cameras in the US in 2003, 28 years later. The first checker's fix ('thirty-seven years before it went bankrupt') adds an off-by-one error. The first picture was taken in December 1975 and the Chapter 11 filing was on 19 January 2012, which is 36 years and about one month apart (computed in Python: about 36.1 years). 2012 minus 1975 only gives 37 if you count from the start of 1975.

history.to: What it couldn't do was make the new thing pay the way the old thing did.
history.reason: The current line states the contested 'innovator's dilemma' cause as settled. Kodak did choose digital: the DCS line from 1991, EasyShare cameras, and number one in US digital camera sales in 2005. Shih (MIT Sloan Management Review, 2016) calls the 'protected film' explanation overblown, and Anthony (HBR, 2016) also disputes it. Nobody disputes that digital cameras earned far thinner margins than film. The first checker's fix is accurate and keeps the voice.

history.reason: The 1975 prototype was never made into a product, and it was first shown publicly in 2001. The invention itself was not hidden: patent US 4,131,919 (Lloyd and Sasson) was filed in 1977 and granted in December 1978, which made it public, and Kodak's digital work went on. The first checker's fix, 'Kodak patented it, and kept quiet', contradicts itself, because a granted patent is a public document.

history.reason: Placed just before 'In January 2012, Kodak filed...', the line puts the camera-sales collapse ahead of the bankruptcy, which gets the order of events wrong. CIPA's global shipments peaked at about 121.5 million in 2010 and were still about 115 million in 2011. Most of the collapse (to 35.4 million by 2015, about 71% down, computed) came after the filing. 'At all' also overstates, because people still buy cameras. The first checker's fix ('most people stopped buying separate cameras') removes 'at all' but keeps the wrong order.

history.reason: Leaving this out is misleading. With the title and 'stayed in the lab', viewers will assume Kodak stayed out of digital cameras. In fact Kodak was America's top digital camera seller in 2005 (IDC: about 24.9% unit share; Kodak's 8-K also claims the number one US position). The first checker marked this optional. It should go in, because the film's argument depends on it.

history.to: It was the first self-contained digital camera.
history.reason: An unqualified 'first' invites the standard correction. The Cromemco Cyclops, a 32x32 MOS-sensor digital camera, was published in Popular Electronics in February 1975, before Sasson's December 1975 picture. Sasson's camera is credited as the first self-contained, portable digital still camera, the one that recorded its own image. The first checker's fix is accurate.

The first checker's 'Almost every' is defensible against the 90% film figure, but that figure is film sales, not photographs, and it comes from secondary sources. 'Most' cannot be challenged.

scriptTitle: How a Chatbot Picks Its Next Word
script:
[A sentence on screen with a blank at the end: "The cat sat on the ___"]
Finish this sentence. You probably said "mat". Maybe "sofa". Almost certainly not "volcano".

[Words appear with bars beside them: mat, sofa, floor, volcano]
You just did, in your head, the one thing a chatbot does. It looks at the words so far and asks: what's likely to come next?

[The sentence breaks into small chunks]
First, it chops the text into small pieces called tokens. A token can be a whole word, or part of one.

[Chunks flow into a box labelled "model"]
Those pieces go into the model: a very large pile of numbers that were adjusted, during training, by reading an enormous amount of text.

[Out comes a list with percentages, labelled "illustrative"]
Out comes a list. Every possible next piece, each with a chance. "Mat", high. "Sofa", lower. "Volcano", nearly zero.

[A spinner whose slices match the bars picks one]
Then it picks one. Usually a likely one, but not always the top one, which is the main reason the same question can get a different answer twice.

[The picked word joins the sentence; the loop repeats]
That piece is added to the sentence. And the whole thing runs again, for the next piece. And the next. A long answer is this one small step, repeated hundreds or even thousands of times.

[A confident-looking but wrong sentence appears]
This also helps explain its strangest habit. At its core, it is built to produce text that sounds likely. Likely and true usually overlap. Not always. When they don't, you get a confident sentence that's simply wrong.

[Title card]
So: it writes one piece at a time, though research suggests it can plan ahead inside, like picking a rhyme before writing the line. And it doesn't look things up unless it's given a tool to do so.

Next: why it makes things up, and what actually reduces it.

history.reason: 'No thinking ahead' contradicts published research. Anthropic's interpretability team says they 'had set out to show that the model didn't plan ahead, and found instead that it did'. In their poetry example, Claude chose the rhyme ('rabbit') before writing the line, and when that word was removed it wrote a line ending in 'habit'. Anthropic also says Claude 'writes text one word at a time', so 'one piece at a time' still holds. Reasoning chatbots also 'think' before answering, though that thinking is written one piece at a time too. The first checker's fix replaces only the fragment 'So: no thinking ahead in sentences,', but its new text repeats the looking-things-up clause. Applied as given, it would leave 'no looking things up unless it's given a tool to do so' in the script twice, so the whole sentence has to be replaced. Their wording 'plan a little ahead' also states as settled what comes from one study of one model (Claude 3.5 Haiku), and it undersells Anthropic's own phrase, 'many words ahead'. 'Research suggests' plus the concrete rhyme example is accurate and keeps the channel's promise to flag what is still uncertain.

history.to: This also helps explain its strangest habit. At its core, it is built to produce text that sounds likely.
history.reason: The script states one cause of hallucination as if it were the whole, settled explanation. OpenAI's 2025 paper 'Why Language Models Hallucinate' (Kalai et al.) agrees that next-word pretraining can't learn arbitrary rare facts from patterns. It also blames training and benchmark grading that reward confident guessing over 'I don't know'. scriptTitle: How Far Is a Light-Year, Really?
script:
[A torch switches on in the dark]
Switch on a torch. The light leaves at about three hundred thousand kilometres every second. In one second it could circle the Earth more than seven times.

[Earth, a line racing to the Moon]
At that speed, the Moon is a little over one second away.

[Line continues to the Sun]
The Sun is about eight minutes and twenty seconds away. So the sunlight on your window right now left the Sun before you started this video.

[Counter spinning: one year]
Now let that light keep going for a whole year. The distance it covers is one light-year: about nine and a half trillion kilometres.

[Text: "A light-year is a distance, not a time."]
That's the part people mix up. A light-year isn't a length of time. It's how far light gets in one.

[Zoom out to a single nearby star]
So how far is the nearest star beyond the Sun? Proxima Centauri is about four and a quarter light-years away. Light, the fastest thing there is, needs more than four years to get there.

[A small probe drifting]
And us? Voyager 1 is the farthest spacecraft we've sent. It travels at roughly seventeen kilometres every second. At that speed, covering the distance to Proxima Centauri would take around seventy-five thousand years. And Voyager isn't even pointed that way.

[Night sky]
One more thing. Because light takes time to arrive, looking far away is looking back in time. Every star you see at night, you see as it was more than four years ago. Most of them, far longer.

[Title card]
That's a light-year. Next time: if there are that many stars, why is the night sky dark?

history.from: You see that star as it was more than four years ago.

history.reason: 'That star' is Proxima Centauri, and this line sits over a [Night sky] shot, so it implies viewers can look up and see it. They can't. Proxima is about magnitude 11.1, around 100 times too faint for the naked eye (computed: 10^(0.4 x 5.1) = 112). At declination -62.7 degrees it also never rises anywhere north of about 27 degrees N. The first checker's fix ('Point a telescope at Proxima Centauri...') is true, but it still fails for most of Europe, the US and China, where Proxima never rises, and it clashes with the night-sky shot. The replacement is true everywhere. The nearest stars you can see without a telescope are Alpha Centauri A and B at about 4.37 light-years, and every star beyond the Sun is at least 4.25 light-years away, so every star in the night sky is seen as it was more than four years ago. Most naked-eye stars are tens to hundreds of light-years away.

history.reason: The title takes for granted that one star is known to be the biggest. There isn't one. scriptTitle: Why the Roman Empire Split in Two
script:
[Map: the Roman Empire around AD 250, one colour]
By the third century, Rome ruled from Britain to Egypt. One empire. And one very large problem: it was too big for one man to run.

[Messenger line crawling across the map]
A message from the Rhine frontier to the Euphrates could take weeks. An emperor fighting on one border couldn't be on the other. And generals who won battles far from Rome kept deciding they should be emperor instead.

[Text: "Diocletian"]
In the 280s, a soldier-emperor named Diocletian turned an old stopgap into a system. Don't hold it all yourself. Share it.

[Map splits into two shades, then four]
He took a co-emperor to rule the West while he held the East. In 293 he went further: two senior emperors and two juniors. Four men, four courts, one empire.

[The four pieces flicker and merge]
It worked while he was there to hold it together. After he retired, rival emperors fought each other for nearly twenty years, and one man came out on top: Constantine.

[A new city appears on the Bosporus]
Constantine did something that mattered more than any battle. In 330 he opened a new capital in the East, on the site of Byzantium. Constantinople. The richest half of the empire now had a Rome of its own.

[Text: "395"]
The empire was joined and divided several more times. Then, in 395, the emperor Theodosius died and left it to his two sons: one took the East, one the West. It was meant to be one empire with two courts. It was never ruled by one man again.

[West fades; East stays]
The western half fell in 476. The eastern half lasted until 1453: almost a thousand years longer.

[Title card]
Rome didn't split because of one decision. It split because the same rough line on the map kept turning out to be useful. Next: the city everyone wanted.

history.note: First drafts written from general knowledge, before any checking.

history.from: After he retired, the four fought each other, and one man came out on top: Constantine.
history.to: After he retired, rival emperors fought each other for nearly twenty years, and one man came out on top: Constantine.
history.reason: The original four tetrarchs did not fight it out among themselves. Diocletian stayed retired and refused to come back at Carnuntum in 308. Constantius died at York in 306, and Galerius died of illness in 311. The civil wars of 306-324 were fought mainly by Constantine, Maxentius, Severus, Maximinus Daia and Licinius. Constantine beat Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge in 312 and Licinius at Chrysopolis in 324. The first checker's fix, 'his successors fought each other', is close but slightly off. Maximian, one of the original four, came out of retirement and fought (alongside Maxentius in 307, then against Constantine in 310), and Galerius invaded Italy in 307. Neither of them was Diocletian's 'successor'. 'Rival emperors' covers everyone involved. Computed: 324 - 305 = 19 years, so 'nearly twenty years' is right.

history.from: One empire, one emperor.
history.to: One empire.
history.reason: Shared rule was normal before Diocletian. Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus ruled jointly from 161. In the third century many emperors made their sons co-Augusti: Septimius Severus with Caracalla and Geta, Philip with Philip II, Decius with Herennius Etruscus, Gallus with Volusianus, Carus with Carinus. Valerian and Gallienus had already split the empire East/West in 253-260, and in 260-274 it broke into three. The first checker's fix, 'usually one emperor', brings in a new problem: for much of the third century there was more than one Augustus at a time. Cutting the clause keeps the rhythm ('One empire. And one very large problem...') and still echoes 'four courts, one empire' later. The list of co-emperors comes from general knowledge, because my own searches were blocked this turn. The Valerian/Gallienus and Carus examples come from the first checker's sources.

history.from: tried a new answer.
history.to: turned an old stopgap into a system.
history.reason: Sharing power, and even an East/West split, was not new. Valerian took the East while Gallienus held the West (253-260), and Carus left Carinus in the West in 283. What Diocletian added was a lasting, organised arrangement: a colleague who was not a relative (Maximian, Caesar 285, Augustus 286), then from 293 four rulers with set ranks and regions. Calling it 'a new answer' would make a knowledgeable viewer wince. The first checker's fix ('took an old answer and made it a system') is accurate too; this wording is a little plainer. Avoid 'permanent': the system collapsed within a few years of 305.

history.from: And one very large problem: it was too big to run.
history.to: And one very large problem: it was too big for one man to run.
history.reason: As written it is false: Rome had run the empire for more than two centuries. The usual explanation for Diocletian's reform is narrower. With wars on several frontiers at once, one emperor could not be everywhere, and armies raised their own commanders. That is what the next lines describe. The first checker's fix is right and adds no new error.

history.from: [Map: the Roman Empire at full size, one colour]
history.to: [Map: the Roman Empire around AD 250, one colour]
history.reason: A 'full size' map means the AD 117 maximum under Trajan. That includes Armenia, Assyria and southern Mesopotamia down to the Persian Gulf, which Hadrian gave up in 117-118. The narration says 'By the third century', so the map should show third-century borders: Severan northern Mesopotamia, with Dacia still held until the 270s. A map dated around AD 250 fits and comes before the Gallic and Palmyrene breakaways (260-274), so one colour is still right. The Dacia abandonment date (Aurelian, c. 271-275) is general knowledge; neither checker confirmed it by search.

history.from: It split because one line on the map kept turning out to be useful.
history.to: It split because the same rough line on the map kept turning out to be useful.
history.reason: The East/West dividing line moved a long way in the Balkans. Under the Tetrarchy, Galerius's eastern share included Pannonia (his seat was Sirmium). After 337 and again after 364, all of Illyricum went with the West. In 379 eastern Illyricum passed to Theodosius, and after 395 Pannonia was western while Dacia and Macedonia were eastern. 'One line' is fair as a metaphor, but the animation must not show one fixed border through every era, and 'rough' says so in the narration. This is a minor point; the first checker's fix is fine too. The Balkan details are general knowledge, not confirmed by search this turn.

history.from: How Mongolia Conquered Half the World in One Lifetime
history.to: How the Mongols Built History's Biggest Land Empire in One Lifetime
history.reason: 'Mongolia' is the modern state; the conquerors were the Mongols. At its peak the Mongol Empire covered about 24 million km². Computed: 24 / 148.9 million km² of world land = 16.12%, about a sixth, not half. It is the largest contiguous empire on record (Guinness), so 'biggest land empire' holds. The British Empire was larger in total, but it was not a contiguous land empire. 'One lifetime' is defensible. Computed: 1206 (Genghis Khan proclaimed) to the c. 1279 peak = 73 years. Kublai, born 1215, lived through nearly all of it.

history.from: Why Egypt Is Shaped Like a River
history.to: Why Almost Everyone in Egypt Lives Along One River
history.reason: The country itself is roughly square, with long straight borders: the 22nd parallel with Sudan and the 25th meridian with Libya. What is river-shaped is where people live. The CIA World Factbook puts about 95% of the population on the Nile valley and delta, about 5% of the land, and the FAO gives a similar figure (about 97% on about 4%). The new title is true at those figures.

history.from: Why Africa's Borders Are So Straight
history.to: Why So Many of Africa's Borders Are Straight
history.reason: The title takes as settled something that is disputed. Estimates of how many African borders are straight lines range widely: Barbour (1961) about 44% along parallels or meridians, Alesina, Easterly and Matuszeski 80%. Paine, Qiu and Ricart-Huguet (American Political Science Review, 2024) argue that rivers, watersheds and earlier states shaped far more of the borders than the 'straight lines' story allows. Every estimate agrees that a large share are straight, more than on other continents, so 'so many' is safe. The channel promises to show both sides, and the video should present that research.

history.from: Where historians disagree, both sides are shown.
history.to: Where historians disagree, the main views and their evidence are shown.
history.reason: Denying or minimising well-documented atrocities ("both sides"): Use the new description line. In scripts, state well-documented atrocities and their death tolls as fact, with sources. Where a government denies one, describe the denial as a political position and say in the narration what historians conclude.

open_questions: My first search hit the session's web-search limit (200 per turn, shared by every agent), so no searches ran. I could not re-check the first checker's confirmations independently online. This review rests on their cited sources, my own general knowledge and my own arithmetic (1453-476 = 977; 324-305 = 19; 24/148.9 = 16.12%; 35.5/148.9 = 23.84%; 1279-1206 = 73; 2026-966 = 1060). A follow-up message would let the search continue, and the points below would be the first to re-search.
Constantinople as a 'new capital' in 330: mainstream encyclopedias say so, but some scholars argue it became the permanent capital only gradually. Consider a description-box note.

476 vs 480 (Julius Nepos) for the end of the West, and whether Diocletian's abdication was voluntary (Lactantius says Galerius pressured him): both belong in the description box under the channel's 'both sides' promise.

The Tetrarchy's four zones were areas of responsibility, not formal states, and scholars disagree about how fixed the Caesars' regions were in 293-305. The '[Map splits into two shades, then four]' visual should avoid hard frontier lines.
Mongol Empire peak: the 24 million km² figure is usually dated c. 1270-1279, after the 1260 break-up into khanates. Whether to count that as 'one empire' should be handled in that video.
The '37% of bilateral borders' figure attributed to Paine, Qiu and Ricart-Huguet comes from press coverage and was not confirmed in the paper itself. Check it before putting it on screen.

'How Britain Ended Up With a Quarter of the Map': the c. 1920 figure (about 35.5 million km², about 24% of land) includes League of Nations mandates, and 'of the map' should be understood as 'of the world's land'. Acceptable as a hook; I made no edit.
'The Empire You've Never Heard Of: Khwarazm' overlaps heavily with the Mongol video (Khwarazm's fall in 1219-1221 is part of that story). Not an error, but a planning note.

scriptTitle: A Quiet Night in a Medieval Monastery (opening)
script:
[Slow fade in: a stone corridor, one candle. Voice low and unhurried. Pause where the lines break.]

Good evening. There is nothing you need to remember tonight, and nothing you need to follow. If you drift off partway through, that is exactly what this is for.

Tonight we are going to spend one night in a monastery, somewhere in Europe, a little under a thousand years ago.

The day here follows a rule written in the sixth century by a man named Benedict. It divides the day, and the night, into work, reading and prayer. It has been followed, more or less, ever since.

It is evening. The last meal has been eaten in silence, while one brother read aloud. The bowls have been wiped and put away.

The brothers walk to the church for the last prayers of the day. The light is going. Nobody hurries.

After this, nobody speaks until morning. It is called the great silence. Doors are closed gently. Sandals are set down side by side.

In the dormitory there is a long row of narrow beds. A straw mattress. A wool blanket. One small lamp is left burning through the night, as the rule asks.

Outside, it is cold, and very dark, in a way that is hard to picture now. There are no lights on the hills. Only stars, and a great many of them.

The brothers sleep in their habits, so that they are ready.

Because later, in the middle of the night, a bell will ring. Softly. And they will get up, in the dark, and walk back down the cold stairs to sing.

But that is not yet.

For now, the lamp burns low. The stone holds the last of the day's warmth. And one by one, along the row, breathing slows.

[Continue at the same pace: the night office, the bakehouse before dawn, the scriptorium at first light.]

scriptTitle: The Day the Mona Lisa Walked Out of the Louvre
script:
[Text on black: "Paris. Monday 21 August 1911."]
On a Monday morning in August 1911, the Louvre was closed to the public. Cleaners and workmen had the building to themselves.

[Illustration: an empty wall with four iron hooks]
By the time anyone looked properly, there was a gap on the wall of the Salon Carré. Four iron hooks, and nothing hanging on them.

[Text: "It took more than a day for anyone to raise the alarm."]
At first, nobody panicked. Paintings were often taken away to be photographed. It was only the next day, when a visiting artist asked where she had gone, that the museum understood. The Mona Lisa had been stolen.

[Newspaper front pages]
The Louvre shut for a week. The borders were watched. The story ran on front pages around the world.

[Two silhouettes]
The police needed suspects. A separate theft of small statues from the Louvre led them to two famous ones. The poet Guillaume Apollinaire was arrested and held for several days. His friend, a young painter named Pablo Picasso, was brought in for questioning. Both were let go. Neither had anything to do with the Mona Lisa.

[A plain trunk in a small room]
For more than two years, the painting was simply gone. In fact it had barely moved. It was in Paris, in the lodgings of an Italian workman named Vincenzo Peruggia, who had once worked at the Louvre.

[Text: "Florence. December 1913."]
In December 1913, Peruggia took it to Florence and offered it to an art dealer. The dealer called in the director of the Uffizi gallery. Then they called the police.

[The painting back on a wall, crowds in front]
Peruggia said he had done it to bring her home to Italy. The painting was back in the Louvre in January 1914. That June, a court in Florence gave him a short prison sentence.

[Title card]
Before the theft, she was a masterpiece. After it, she was on her way to becoming the most famous painting in the world. Next: how he got it out of the building.

history.to: The painting was back in the Louvre in January 1914. That June, a court in Florence gave him a short prison sentence.
history.reason: The order of events is wrong, and the date is shaky. The painting was rehung in the Louvre on 4 January 1914, after being shown in Florence, Rome and Milan. Peruggia was not tried until 4 to 5 June 1914 in Florence (1 year 15 days, cut on appeal to about 7 months 9 days). The current wording puts the sentence before the return. 'Back to Paris in early 1914' may also be literally wrong: the special train is usually said to have reached Paris on 31 December 1913 (I could not confirm this). Anchoring on the Louvre in January 1914 avoids that. I agree with the first checker's diagnosis but not their wording. 'That summer, he was tried in Florence and served a short sentence' suggests he served the time after the trial. In fact he had been in custody since his arrest on 11 or 12 December 1913 and was freed in July 1914, mostly on time already served (custody plus 7 months 9 days ends about 20 to 21 July 1914, computed in Python). 'Gave him a short prison sentence' is accurate either way.

history.to: The police needed suspects. A separate theft of small statues from the Louvre led them to two famous ones.

Géry Pieret, Apollinaire's former secretary, had stolen Iberian statuettes from the Louvre, sold two to Picasso and boasted about it to Paris-Journal on 29 August 1911. That trail led to Apollinaire's arrest on 7 September. The first checker's own evidence records this link but still passed the line. Also, in 1911 Picasso was known in the art world, not to the public at large.

Naming the Mona Lisa keeps the exoneration exactly true, which matters for a channel that promises 'no guessing about guilt'.

script:
[A bill appears: $3,000]
Here's a repair bill for three thousand dollars. You have insurance. So who pays?

[The bill splits into two bars]
The answer is usually "both of you", and the word that decides the split is the deductible.

[First bar labelled "You: $500"]
A deductible is the part of a covered loss that you pay yourself before the insurance pays anything. Say yours is five hundred dollars.

[Second bar labelled "Insurer: $2,500"]
On this three-thousand-dollar bill, you pay the first five hundred. The insurer pays the remaining two thousand five hundred. This is a made-up example: real policies have limits and exclusions, and they differ.

[A smaller bill: $400]
Now a smaller bill. Four hundred dollars. That's under your deductible, so the insurer pays nothing. On a car or home policy, there's usually no point in claiming, though after a car accident your policy may still require you to report it.

[Seesaw: deductible on one side, premium on the other]
So why would anyone choose a bigger deductible? Because of the seesaw. The premium is what you pay to have the policy. In general, the more of each loss you agree to carry yourself, the lower the premium. A higher deductible usually means a lower premium, and the other way round.

[Calendar]
One more thing to check on your own policy: when the deductible applies. On many car and home policies, it applies each time you claim. On many health plans, it adds up across a year, so smaller bills for covered care still count toward it, and some care, like a check-up, is often paid for by the plan before you reach it. The policy itself says which.

[Checklist]
So, three questions to ask of any policy: How much is the deductible? Does it apply per claim or per year? And could I actually pay it tomorrow if I had to?

[Title card]
This is general education, not advice about your policy. Next: premium, deductible and copay, in one picture.

scriptTitle: How to make the first recording (no script needed)
script:
This channel has no narration, so here is the recipe instead.

1. Sound. Record the main sound of each video yourself where you can. A licensed sound can be one layer in your own mix, never the whole video with little change: a licence settles copyright, but YouTube's reused-content rule applies even with permission, and the same library rain can be on many other channels. Keep every licence. Never use sound copied from another channel.

2. Loop. Build a section of at least 10 to 15 minutes before it repeats, with crossfades so the join can't be heard. A short loop is easy to notice and reads as low effort.

3. Level. Keep the volume even from start to end. No thunderclap louder than the rest. No fade-in that starts silent.

4. Picture. One still image or a black screen. Use a photo you took or one licensed for commercial use, and keep the licence: a picture found online isn't yours to monetize. Say "black screen" in the title when it is one: people search for it.

5. Length. Give each sound one length, anywhere from 2 to 10 hours (YouTube's upload limit is 12 hours). Don't upload the same mix again at another length: two videos of the same sound can look interchangeable, and YouTube doesn't monetize channels where videos feel interchangeable.

6. Make each video its own thing. A different place, different layers, a different picture. Ten uploads of the same rain with new titles is exactly what the inauthentic-content rule is aimed at.

7. Description. Say what the sounds are, where and how you recorded them, what you layered together and how long the loop is, and credit any licensed sound. YouTube's reviewers may read descriptions to see how you made the content. Don't claim it treats insomnia, anxiety or any condition.

scriptTitle: The Snail Who Was Late for Work (30-second storyboard)
script:
No dialogue. Sound: a ticking clock, traffic, one muted trumpet line. Cinematic, muted colours: early-morning blue, office fluorescent.

0-2s  HOOK. Extreme close-up: a phone the size of a billboard lights up beside a sleeping snail. 08:52. Its eye stalks shoot up.

2-6s  It throws on a tiny tie, grabs a coffee cup the size of its shell, and slides out of the door. Wide shot: the office building is across a six-lane road.

6-11s  It sets off. A bus thunders past. The coffee wobbles. A pigeon lands, looks at it, and leaves, unimpressed.

11-16s  Rain. Every other commuter runs for cover; the snail, for once, speeds up on the wet tarmac. A small, private smile.

16-22s  The lift is out of order. It looks up the stairwell, sighs, and starts climbing.

22-27s  It reaches the meeting room, damp and triumphant, and pushes the door open. Empty chairs. On the screen: "MEETING MOVED TO 08:30".

27-30s  END. It sets the coffee down, takes the best chair, and puts its feet up. Loop point: the phone lights up again: "Saturday".

Notes: keep this snail as the channel's recurring face, but give every episode its own situation and its own ending. YouTube refuses to monetize characters "put in the same situation over and over again with the same outcome". Write one line per episode (concept and ending) before animating, and check that no two share an arc. Keep thumbnails, titles and tags free of kid-targeted wording, toy-like styling and nursery colours.

from.scriptTitle: The Snail Who Crossed the Road (30-second storyboard)
from.script:
No dialogue. Music: one soft marimba line that grows.

0-2s  HOOK. Ground level. A tiny snail with a small red flag on its shell looks across a huge grey road. On the far side: one green leaf.

2-6s  It takes a breath and sets off. A wide shot shows how far it is. Almost nothing has changed.

6-11s  A bicycle wheel rolls past, enormous. The snail ducks into its shell. A pause. One eye comes back out.

11-16s  Rain starts. The snail brightens: the road is wet, so it glides faster. Its first small smile.

16-21s  A puddle blocks the way. It looks left, then right, then climbs onto a floating leaf and paddles with its flag.

21-26s  The far kerb: a wall, from down here. It tries. Slides back. Tries again. Slides back. Plants the flag in a crack and pulls itself up.

26-29s  It reaches the green leaf, and stops. Another, smaller snail is already there, waiting. They share the leaf.

29-30s  END CARD. The red flag, planted beside the leaf. Loop point: the camera tilts up to the road, matching the first frame.

Notes: keep this snail and its flag in every episode so the channel has one character people recognise. Design it yourself; don't base it on an existing character.
